newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian turmoil could let Pol Pot off the hook.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian turmoil could let Pol Pot off the hook.

text.p: The chances of bringing Khmer Rouge guerrilla chief Pol Pot to justice may have evaporated with the violent collapse of the fragile coalition government at the weekend, analysts said on Tuesday.
First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh had been seeking to secure Pol Pot's handover in negotiations with a Khmer Rouge faction believed to be holding him.
But the bloody rupture of the coalition government and ouster of Ranarridh all but killed off chances Pol Pot would be brought to justice, the analysts said.
"You can forget it. That chance has been completely lost for now," said a Cambodian political analyst. "The only way we would have ever seen Pol Pot alive was if we had a united govermnment."

Pol Pot, mastermind of the 1975-79 "killing fields" regime which led to more than a million deaths, was captured by the guerrilla faction which had broken with him after a violent split in the Maoist group's leadership in May.

The enigmatic Pol Pot is now believed to be seriously ill and held in the Khmer Rouge's former northern stronghold at Anlong Veng. Before Ranariddh's ouster, his aides said they were on the verge of bringing Pol Pot out for trial.
Fighting erupted between forces loyal to the country's two premiers on Saturday, a day after Ranariddh had left the country.
Troops under powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen took control of the capital on Monday, hours after he had announced he was unilaterally ousting Ranariddh as first prime minister.

The two premiers headed a coalition government formed after a 1993 election organised by the United Nations. Their relations began to deteriorate sharply last year over a power-sharing row and turned icy earlier this year when Ranariddh announced he had opened peace talks with the Khmer Rouge.

Ranariddh said he was willing to form a political alliance with less-tarnished Khmer Rouge figures, infuriating Hun Sen, whom analysts said wanted to prevent any deal which would bolster his political rival's position.
Hun Sen declared the prince's negotiations with the Khmer Rouge illegal.
"Without a united government there will be no more negotiation with the Khmer Rouge," the Cambodian analyst said.
Others agreed that the break-up of the coalition meant the end of talks with the rebels.
"This cuts off negotiations with the Khmer Rouge but it's just too complicated now to say what might happen," said a western political analyst.

Ranariddh's top military man, General Nhiek Bun Chhay, had spearheaded talks with the breakaway rebel faction. The general fled from Phnom Penh on Sunday night after two days of heavy fighting in the capital.
